text: But a transition system depends on the opponent giving you somewhere to transition into. When the other team advances, Carrick's United can compress the centre, win the next ball, and attack before the block resets. When the opponent sits deeper, the picture changes. United need repeatable possession patterns: a full-back who knows when to advance, a midfielder who protects the counter, and a front four who create width without abandoning the centre. Early this season, those relationships have looked improvised. The attackers can become too high and too wide. Bruno and Matheus Cunha roam toward the ball. The double pivot is asked to cover an enormous pitch. One lost pass, and the back line is defending a race rather than a structure. This is why the problem cannot be reduced to one player missing or one midfielder having a bad afternoon. The spacing changes from phase to phase. In possession, United need enough width to move the block, enough occupation between the lines to pin the centre-backs, and enough protection behind the ball to survive the first clearance. When one of those disappears, the other two become liabilities. The team looks organised until the next action asks it to reorganise.
